reviews.scope: explaining why the exterior angle sum is 360 degrees
reviews.reason: The usual derivation subtracts (n-2)x180 from n supplementary pairs. The result can also be justified independently, and finding regular polygon side counts needs only the 360 fact.
reviews.counterexample: Walking around the polygon and accumulating turning angles gives one full turn of 360 degrees without the interior sum formula.

reviews.scope: quadrilateral vocabulary and diagonals in the bisecting-diagonals property
reviews.reason: The property that diagonals bisect each other, and talk of opposite sides and angles, presuppose the polygon vocabulary of vertices, sides, angles and diagonals.

reviews.scope: proving parallelogram properties
reviews.reason: Proving opposite sides equal or diagonals bisecting requires drawing a diagonal, selecting ASA or AAS congruence, and writing a complete formal argument. This is exactly the content of the prerequisite.

reviews.scope: parallelogram definition and criteria as converses of properties
reviews.reason: This node bundles the parallelogram definition that the criteria target. Understanding the criteria as converse statements, and combining them in proofs, rests on knowing the properties first.

reviews.scope: proving parallelogram criteria from the definition
reviews.reason: Every criterion must conclude that both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Proofs obtain this through equal alternate interior angles from congruent triangles, which is a parallel-line criterion.

reviews.scope: proving the midsegment theorem
reviews.reason: The textbook proof doubles the midsegment and shows a parallelogram via one pair of sides parallel and equal. Stating and applying the theorem do not need this.
reviews.counterexample: Prove the theorem with SAS similarity at ratio 1:2, or with coordinates of the midpoints, without any parallelogram criterion.

reviews.scope: definition of midsegment via side midpoints
reviews.reason: A midsegment is defined as the segment joining two side midpoints. Halving lengths in computations also uses the midpoint relation, so the midpoint concept is indispensable.

reviews.scope: inherited properties, diagonals bisect each other
reviews.reason: A rectangle is defined as a parallelogram with a right angle. Its diagonals bisecting each other and its opposite sides being equal are inherited parallelogram properties.

reviews.scope: proof via completing the rectangle, as stated in the criteria
reviews.reason: The criterion explicitly asks for the rectangle proof. Completing the right triangle to a rectangle uses equal diagonals that bisect each other.

reviews.scope: meaning of median to the hypotenuse
reviews.reason: The theorem concerns the segment from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse midpoint. The general triangle median definition is needed to identify that segment.

reviews.scope: rectangle definition and criteria as converses
reviews.reason: The rectangle definition lives in this node. The diagonal criterion is the converse of the equal-diagonal property, so learners need the property direction to understand and test it.

reviews.scope: applying parallelogram-based rectangle criteria
reviews.reason: Two of the three criteria take a parallelogram as hypothesis. Using them in proofs therefore requires first establishing a parallelogram with parallelogram criteria.

reviews.scope: rhombus as parallelogram; inherited diagonal bisection
reviews.reason: A rhombus is a parallelogram with equal adjacent sides. The fact that its diagonals bisect each other, which underlies the perpendicular bisection property, is inherited from parallelograms.

reviews.scope: proving diagonals perpendicular and bisecting angles
reviews.reason: Applying three-lines-coincide to the isosceles triangle formed by two sides is one common proof. Congruence offers an equally standard route.
reviews.counterexample: SSS congruence of the four small triangles directly gives equal adjacent angles at the center, hence right angles, and bisected vertex angles.

reviews.scope: computing side length from diagonals
reviews.reason: Side length from half-diagonals needs a squared-sum relation, and such problems are frequent. Stating properties and computing area from diagonals do not use the theorem.
reviews.counterexample: Area equals half the product of diagonals, and side from perimeter needs no Pythagorean theorem.

reviews.scope: rhombus definition and criteria as converses
reviews.reason: The rhombus definition is in the properties node. The perpendicular-diagonals criterion is the converse of a stated property, so recognizing and justifying it builds on knowing the property.

reviews.scope: applying parallelogram-hypothesis rhombus criteria; four-equal-sides proof
reviews.reason: Two criteria assume a parallelogram, which must be established first. The four-equal-sides criterion is proved through the two-pairs-of-equal-opposite-sides parallelogram criterion.

reviews.scope: proving the perpendicular-diagonals criterion
reviews.reason: One diagonal perpendicularly bisects the other, so the bisector property gives equal adjacent sides. This is one convenient proof path, not the only one.
reviews.counterexample: SAS congruence of two triangles on either side of a diagonal gives equal adjacent sides without the bisector theorem.

reviews.scope: square criteria and inclusion diagram
reviews.reason: Square criteria typically take a rectangle plus equal adjacent sides. The inclusion diagram places squares inside rectangles, so rectangle criteria and concepts are needed.

reviews.scope: square criteria and inclusion diagram
reviews.reason: Squares are characterized as rhombuses with a right angle. The inclusion relations position squares within rhombuses, so rhombus criteria are integral to this node.

reviews.scope: folding and moving-point problems in square settings
reviews.reason: The node explicitly includes square backgrounds, where equal sides and right angles drive the equations. Square properties are therefore necessary across that stated scope.

reviews.scope: setting up equations for lengths after folding
reviews.reason: Folding problems set the folded length as x and form a right triangle equation. Applying the Pythagorean theorem in folding contexts is exactly what the prerequisite trains.

reviews.scope: identifying variables and constants in processes
reviews.reason: Classifying which quantities change and which stay fixed is conceptual. Familiarity with expressions helps when processes are given by formulas, but it is not necessary.
reviews.counterexample: Identify time and temperature as variables, and the city as constant, from a weather table without writing any expression.

reviews.scope: definition of function between two variables
reviews.reason: The function definition is stated as a correspondence between two variables in a changing process. Recognizing variables is therefore built into the definition itself.

reviews.scope: viewing correspondence as ordered input-output pairs
reviews.reason: Ordered pairs give an analogy for pairing each x with its y, and the order emphasizes input versus output. The function concept is still definable without them.
reviews.counterexample: Judge uniqueness of correspondence from a rule or table without ever writing ordered pairs.

reviews.scope: meaning of independent variable domain
reviews.reason: The domain is the set of allowed values of the independent variable. That notion only makes sense once a function and its independent variable are understood.

reviews.scope: domain restrictions from denominators
reviews.reason: The node explicitly includes denominators not being zero. Finding domains of fractional formulas uses exactly the algebraic-fraction meaningfulness condition.

reviews.scope: domain restrictions from square roots
reviews.reason: The node explicitly requires a nonnegative radicand. That is precisely the condition for a square root expression to be defined, so this domain case needs it.

reviews.scope: meaning of function value and its inverse lookup
reviews.reason: A function value is the unique y matched to a given x. Interpreting it, and finding x from y, presupposes the correspondence concept.

reviews.scope: computing values from analytic formulas
reviews.reason: Computing function values from a formula means substituting x, including negatives and fractions, and evaluating in the correct order. This is precisely the expression-evaluation skill.

reviews.scope: tabulating points and reading values from graphs
reviews.reason: Plotting by table requires computing function values. Reading the graph also means interpreting a point's ordinate as the function value at its abscissa.

reviews.scope: plotting and reading points of the graph
reviews.reason: Function graphs here are sets of points (x, y) drawn in rectangular coordinates. Plotting and reading them demands locating points by coordinates.

reviews.scope: reading trends from graphs
reviews.reason: Trend charts give informal experience reading change over time from a picture. This transfers to describing increase and decrease on function graphs, but it is not necessary.
reviews.counterexample: Read rises and falls directly from plotted coordinate points without prior trend-chart instruction.

reviews.scope: graph representation and conversions to it
reviews.reason: The graph is one of the three representations. Converting a formula or table into a graph, and comparing advantages, requires graphing ability.

reviews.scope: writing real-world function formulas and domains
reviews.reason: Modeling mainly requires writing an analytic formula and considering the real-world domain. Fluency converting among tables and graphs helps analysis, but it is not necessary.
reviews.counterexample: Write y=5x+20 for total cost and restrict x to nonnegative integers without studying representation conversions.

reviews.scope: generalizing a varying quantity into a formula
reviews.reason: Writing nth-term expressions for patterns rehearses generalizing a relationship symbolically. That supports writing function formulas, though many contexts give the relation directly.
reviews.counterexample: Write area as a function of side length directly from a geometric formula, with no sequence pattern.

reviews.scope: recognizing y=kx and interpreting k
reviews.reason: Primary-school constant-ratio experience gives intuition for k as a fixed ratio. However, recognizing y=kx and graphing it can be learned from the definition alone.
reviews.counterexample: Define proportional functions by the form y=kx, compute k from one point, and graph it without prior ratio lessons.

reviews.scope: graphing and identifying proportional functions
reviews.reason: Graphing y=kx needs function concept and graphing skill. Explicit study of the three representations and their trade-offs is helpful context rather than necessary.
reviews.counterexample: Tabulate and plot y=2x using graphing skills alone, without studying representation advantages and conversions.

reviews.scope: linear function definition and parameters
reviews.reason: Proportional functions are the customary stepping stone and the b=0 special case. The general form y=kx+b can be defined and used directly.
reviews.counterexample: Introduce y=kx+b first, determine k and b from conditions, and note proportional functions afterward as b=0.

reviews.scope: graphing y=kx+b by two points
reviews.reason: Graphing requires recognizing the formula y=kx+b and substituting x values. The concept of a linear function is therefore the object being graphed.

reviews.scope: finding intersections with the coordinate axes
reviews.reason: Finding axis intercepts uses the fact that points on the x-axis have y=0 and points on the y-axis have x=0. That fact belongs to this prerequisite.

reviews.scope: interpreting k as tilt and b as y-intercept
reviews.reason: The properties are phrased in graph terms such as inclination direction, y-axis intercept and quadrants passed. These presuppose knowing the graph is a line.

reviews.scope: translating the line y=kx+b
reviews.reason: Translating a graph presumes knowing the graph is a straight line determined by k and b. Only then can one explain why translation preserves k.

reviews.scope: deriving y=kx+b±m from vertical shift
reviews.reason: Shifting each point up m adds m to its ordinate, which directly yields the new formula. This is the coordinate description of translation.

reviews.scope: setting up y=kx+b with unknowns
reviews.reason: The method starts by assuming the general form y=kx+b and substituting known points. Knowing what parameters define a linear function is indispensable.

reviews.scope: solving the system for k and b
reviews.reason: Some elimination method is needed, and substitution is one valid route. The generic need is solving a two-variable system, not substitution specifically.
reviews.counterexample: Subtract the two point equations to eliminate b immediately, using addition-subtraction elimination instead.

reviews.scope: solving the system for k and b
reviews.reason: Subtracting the equations k*x1+b and k*x2+b eliminates b efficiently. This is one solving route, interchangeable with substitution.
reviews.counterexample: Express b from one equation and substitute into the other instead.

reviews.scope: reading equation solution as x-intercept
reviews.reason: The link identifies the solution with the x-coordinate where the line meets the x-axis. That requires understanding the line graph and its axis intersection.

reviews.scope: relating kx+b=0 solution to graph
reviews.reason: The criteria require reading the solution from the graph and explaining the link, which needs the meaning of an equation solution. The full transposition procedure for ax+b=cx+d is not needed.
reviews.counterexample: Read x=2 from the intercept of y=-x+2 and verify by substitution without transposition and combining procedures.

reviews.scope: reading solution sets from graph position
reviews.reason: The solution set is read as the x-range where the line lies above or below the x-axis. This requires understanding and reading line graphs.

reviews.scope: writing inequality solution sets from graphs
reviews.reason: Graphical reading needs the meaning of a solution set and interval notation. The algebraic solving procedure is a parallel route useful for checking, not a necessity.
reviews.counterexample: Read x<2 as the part of y=-x+2 above the x-axis without performing algebraic steps.

reviews.scope: interpreting intersection of two lines
reviews.reason: Interpreting a system solution as the intersection of two lines requires knowing each linear equation corresponds to a line graph.

reviews.scope: identifying intersection with common solution
reviews.reason: The key claim is that the common solution of both equations is the intersection point. The meaning of a system's solution is therefore essential.

reviews.scope: computing intersections by solving systems
reviews.reason: Computing an intersection needs some algebraic solving method. Substitution is natural when both lines are in y= form, but addition-subtraction elimination works equally well.
reviews.counterexample: Subtract one equation from the other to eliminate y, then solve, using addition-subtraction elimination.
